content: Chlorhexidine gluconate is an antibacterial cleansing agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of gingivitis, periodontitis, and for use in skin cleansing procedures. Common side effects include staining of teeth and other oral surfaces, calculus formation, and changes in taste perception. For adults, the FDA-approved indication is the treatment of gingivitis, characterized by redness, swelling of the gingivae, and gingival bleeding upon probing. The recommended dosage is 15 mL of undiluted Paroex® used as an oral rinse for 30 seconds, twice daily, after toothbrushing in the morning and evening. Off-label uses in adults include conditions such as alveolitis of the jaw, burns, nosocomial infectious diseases (including catheter-related infections), dental procedures, prosthetic dental implants, oral infections, and prophylaxis for nosocomial infections or heart operations. However, there is limited information regarding guideline-supported off-label uses. In pediatric patients, the safety and effectiveness of chlorhexidine gluconate have not been established for those under 18 years of age. There is also limited information on off-label uses in pediatric populations. Paroex® is contraindicated in individuals with known hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine gluconate or other formulation ingredients. It is not intended for ingestion and should be expectorated after rinsing. Warnings include the lack of established effects on periodontitis and the potential for increased supragingival calculus formation. Clinical testing has shown that 56% of users experienced measurable increases in facial anterior stain after six months, compared to 35% of control users. Heavy staining occurred in 15% of users, compared to 1% of controls. Staining is more pronounced in patients with heavier plaque accumulation and can generally be removed by professional prophylaxis, though additional time may be required. Patients with anterior facial restorations with rough surfaces or margins should be prescribed with caution, as staining may be difficult to remove and could necessitate restoration replacement. Rare cases of permanent taste alteration and serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Oral irritation and local allergy-type symptoms have also been noted. Post-marketing reports include symptoms such as stomatitis, gingivitis, glossitis, ulcers, dry mouth, hypesthesia, glossal edema, and paresthesia. Parotid gland swelling and salivary gland inflammation (sialadenitis) have also been reported. Chlorhexidine gluconate is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with most of the ingested drug excreted in feces (~90%) and less than 1% in urine. Approximately 30% of the active ingredient is retained in the oral cavity after rinsing and is slowly released into oral fluids. In animal studies, no evidence of teratogenic effects or impaired fertility was observed at high doses. However, adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking, and the drug should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. It is not known whether chlorhexidine gluconate is excreted in human milk, so caution is advised when administering to nursing mothers. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of chlorhexidine gluconate in populations such as geriatric patients, specific genders, racial groups, or those with renal or hepatic impairment. Similarly, there is no established guidance for immunocompromised patients. Paroex® is supplied as a pink liquid in 4 fl oz (118 mL) and 16 fl oz (473 mL) amber plastic bottles with child-resistant caps. It should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F), with permitted excursions to 15°C to 30°C (59°F to 86°F). Patients should be instructed not to rinse with water or other mouthwashes, brush teeth, or eat immediately after using Paroex®. Alcohol interaction with chlorhexidine gluconate has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use with this medication.
